Timorous

/TIM-er-uhs/ - the stress falls on TIM · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Timorous means timid and easily frightened.

The timorous understudy rehearsed brilliantly and then hid in the wings whenever the director glanced her way.

Worked Example

Everyone agreed Dev knew the material cold, yet he was too timorous for the debate club itself: he sat nearest the exit, jumped whenever the timer buzzed, and finally entered a practice round only by passing his argument to a teammate to read aloud.

Timorous points at temperament: not one scared moment but a standing readiness to be frightened. 'Cautious' weighs a risk and proceeds; timorous shrinks back before the risk is even real.

How Timorous Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

fearful

fearful: feeling fear in the moment; timorous makes it a standing temperament

skittish

skittish: nervy and easily startled, said of horses and people alike

Antonyms

bold

bold: ready to act where others hold back

fearless

fearless: untouched by fear altogether

How Strong Is It? — wary → timorous → cowardly

wary vs. timorous

wary vs. timorous: Wary stops short of timorous — the wary keep sensible watch, while the timorous startle at shadows.

cowardly vs. timorous

cowardly vs. timorous: Cowardly goes further than timorous — the timorous feel fear everywhere, but the cowardly let it override duty.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — timor-

Root — timor-: fear (Latin timor, from timere, to fear)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Timor- (fear) + -ous = full of fear. Latin timere, 'to fear,' gave English a small family: timid, the everyday cousin, and timorous, the slightly grander portrait of a person built around their fear.

Use the root in a new word: intimidate

Use the root in a new word: intimidate: The champion's slow warm-up routine was designed to intimidate every challenger watching.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Timorous paints fearfulness as character — the mouse in the fable. Everyday 'timid' or 'shy' is plainer. Keep it apart from its unit-mate tremulous, which names the visible shiver rather than the temperament: a timorous witness may answer in a tremulous voice.
